summary:
South Jeolla has no separate local ordinance on gender identity or gender expression, so a visitor to the province stands under South Korea's national framework. Being transgender is not a criminal offence in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available without surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria; the court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed her personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court ruling at the Pohang branch had already awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom.

Facilities remain a practical risk rather than a legal one. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41 per cent used a restroom of a different gender, 39 per cent avoided food and drink to do so, and 36 per cent went without using a restroom at all.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation in South Jeolla carry no statutory protection on these grounds. The National Human Rights Commission flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023 after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, although the Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling extended recognition of same-sex partners' healthcare rights in that specific area. Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in South Korea alongside a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society, and organised conservative opposition remains active. No severe incident involving a trans visitor in South Jeolla appears in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
South Jeolla is one province among South Korea's seventeen first-level administrative units, and the rules that shape a trans visitor's expectations here are national rather than provincial: the criminal-law position, the document-change procedure, the restroom ruling and the absence of an anti-discrimination statute apply identically across the country. The province contributes no separate legal layer and no documented incident of its own.

The two principal rulings that define the current position came from courts outside the province, a Yeongdong regional court in May 2024 and a Seoul appellate court in July 2024, which indicates that the shift is a nationwide judicial pattern rather than a local policy. Enforcement of the restroom right has also been tested in Daegu, in the country's south-east.

Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are described as broadly positive for visitors, but they are a Seoul phenomenon and should not be assumed to transfer to provincial cities in South Jeolla, where venues and community presence are thinner. The surrounding national context still requires care: no anti-discrimination law, active conservative opposition, and documented discrimination recorded by Human Rights Watch in 2025.
localsOnly:
South Korean citizens can petition a family court to change their registered sex, and since the May 2024 Yeongdong ruling the courts no longer treat sex-reassignment surgery as a prerequisite; hormone therapy and a demonstrated life lived in the acquired gender have supported applications, and judicial guidelines requiring surgery now serve only as reference. The Supreme Court has also permitted a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Transgender people are excluded from military service, and service members who have sex with a partner of the same sex face up to two years' imprisonment under Military Criminal Act article 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023. A gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017.

Residents have a damages remedy where police or institutions obstruct restroom access: the 300,000 won award finalised in July 2024 ran against the state, and the 7 million won award of 2021 ran against a private beauty academy. The National Human Rights Commission of Korea accepts complaints and has publicly pressed the Ministry of Health and Welfare on hospitalisation guidance for transgender patients.

Employment, housing and access to services are unprotected on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation because no comprehensive anti-discrimination law is in force. Same-sex couples cannot marry, though the Constitutional Court's 2024 decision gives same-sex partners standing in health-insurance decisions.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record any incident involving a trans visitor in South Jeolla, so the province-level risk picture rests on the national framework rather than on local evidence; local policing practice, venue access and hospital willingness in Jeonju, Yeosu or Mokpo are not sourced here.

Whether the Yeongdong approach to surgery-free document change has been applied uniformly by courts hearing petitions from South Jeolla is unresolved in these materials, as is the current caseload or approval rate for such petitions.

The practical availability of gender-neutral or single-occupancy restrooms in South Jeolla's transport hubs, hotels and public buildings is not sourced, and the 2021 National Human Rights Commission survey does not break its findings down by province.

Human Rights Watch's 2025 reporting is national in scope and does not isolate South Korea's southern provinces, so the discrimination it documents cannot be attributed to this jurisdiction specifically.
